URGENT BUG (customer-affecting, reported 2026-10-02 by a creator partner): every Nxeon Terraria server runs the image `ryshe/terraria:latest` (sha256:b1c89f7f...), i.e. TShock 6.1.0.0 / Terraria server v1.4.5.6 (lib/terraria-plugins.ts documents the layout: container and unit `terraria`, /opt/terraria mounted at /tshock/tshock and the Worlds folder, plugins at /tshock/CustomPlugins with `-additionalplugins`, bootstrap.sh in the image). The current Terraria game client is 1.4.5.8 and TShock 6.2.1 is the release that supports it (https://github.com/Pryaxis/TShock/releases/tag/v6.2.1). Players on the current client cannot join our servers (version mismatch). There are 3 Terraria servers today (one on the primary, two on node-5, one is a paying customer's). The platform also has NO update path for docker-based families like Terraria (see the comments near lib/game-update*.ts line ~426: 'no update path').
DO:
1. Research the correct, MAINTAINED way to run TShock 6.2.1 / Terraria 1.4.5.8 in Docker today: the official image (ghcr.io/pryaxis/tshock and its tags/args/volumes/entrypoint; check the TShock repo's Dockerfile, README and docs) versus continuing with ryshe/terraria (is it maintained? does it have a newer tag?). Establish the exact container contract of the chosen image: entrypoint, args (-world, -autocreate, -worldname, -port, -maxplayers, -password, -config, -configpath, -worldpath, -logpath, -additionalplugins), volumes (worlds, config, logs, plugins), env vars, ports, and how the world file name/path and config.json location differ from ryshe's. Also confirm the world-file and TShock config/db compatibility from 1.4.5.6/TShock 6.1 to 1.4.5.8/6.2.1 so existing worlds and config survive.
2. Build an UPDATE path for existing servers (new function in the worker, wired as a GAME_UPDATE for terraria, reusing worker/game-config-appliers/kit/env-recreate.ts): back up /opt/terraria (worlds + config.json + db) to a timestamped copy on the guest, pull the new image, recreate the container with the SAME volumes, ports and settings but the new image/entrypoint adapted to the new contract, start it, wait for the port with the slow-start window, verify the running versions from the container's own log lines ('TShock v6.2.x', 'Terraria Server v1.4.5.8') and that the world loaded, and roll back to the old container/image and backups on any failure. Never lose a world. A server the customer stopped stays stopped (update the image and recreate but leave it stopped).
3. Update the Terraria OsTemplate setup script / provisioning bake and the Terraria applier (worker/game-config-appliers/terraria.ts, lib/game-applier-specs/terraria.ts) so NEW servers and the settings applier work with the new image contract; pin the image to an explicit version tag or digest (never `latest` for a game server) and add a single place (setting or constant) where the pinned Terraria/TShock version lives so future updates are a one-line change. Add a sweep or admin check that compares each Terraria server's running version against the pinned one and reports drift (report only, no auto-update).
4. Tests with fakes (update success, rollback on failed start, stopped server stays stopped, world files untouched, version verification parsing), typecheck, docs section. Include in your report the exact owner rollout steps: one-by-one update of the 3 servers starting with a throwaway, what to check, and how to roll back. Report per the brief, including what you could not verify (a real update was NOT run).

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. Only the page itself is wrapped in a document skeleton at publish time: an HTML file in `files` is another page served without one, so Claude starts each with its own `<!doctype html>`, charset and viewport metas and base styles, or, without the doctype, it renders in quirks mode with browser defaults. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

#!/bin/bash
# Two-slot lock so at most TWO heavy jobs (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) run at once on this box.
# This machine is the live production primary (also hosts customer VMs) — uncontrolled parallel tsc/dev servers
# can OOM or starve production. (Was 1 slot; raised to 2 on 2026-10-01 because 20 agents were queueing.)
# usage: heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-foo && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."
deadline=$((SECONDS + 3600))
while [ $SECONDS -lt $deadline ]; do
  for i in 1 2; do
    exec {fd}>/tmp/nxeon-heavy.$i.lock
    if flock -n $fd; then
      exec nice -n 19 ionice -c3 env NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=3072" "$@"
    fi
    exec {fd}>&-
  done
  sleep 2
done
echo "heavy.sh: timed out waiting for a slot" >&2; exit 75

18775:## Game config appliers
18776-
18777-(Added 2026-10-02, branch `feature/game-config-apply-core`. Owner requirement: every game's Settings page must either really change the running server, surviving restarts and reinstalls, or say honestly that it cannot.)
18778-
18779-### What it is
18780-
18781-A small framework so each game family's Settings save really reaches the game, one file per family. The older inline appliers in `worker/game-config.ts` (minecraft, rust, valheim, palworld, bedrock, cs2, dayz, fivem, plus `worker/zomboid-admin.ts`) are untouched and still win: `applyRealConfig` only dispatches to the registry in its `default:` case.
18782-
18783-| Piece | File | Runs in |
18784-|---|---|---|
18785-| Spec: which schema fields are handled, and how each takes effect | `lib/game-applier-specs/<family>.ts` | client + worker (pure, no I/O) |
18786-| Spec list (ONE line per family) + helpers | `lib/game-config-appliers.ts` (`APPLIER_SPECS`) | client + worker |
18787-| Applier code | `worker/game-config-appliers/<family>.ts` | worker |
18788-| Registry (ONE line per family) | `worker/game-config-appliers/index.ts` | worker |
18789-| Runner (changed-field filter, no-op, redaction, never throws) | `worker/game-config-appliers/run.ts` | worker |
18790-| Kit: `kit/json-patch.ts`, `kit/ini-patch.ts`, `kit/kv-patch.ts`, `kit/config-file.ts`, `kit/env-recreate.ts`, `kit/readback.ts` | `worker/game-config-appliers/kit/` | worker |
18791-| Shared types (`Guest`, `ApplierContext`, `ApplyOutcome`, `GameConfigApplier`) | `worker/game-config-appliers/types.ts` | worker |
18792-| Test fake (files + tiny docker/systemd) | `test/_fake-docker-guest.ts` | tests |
18793-
18794-**Per-field honesty is derived, never hand-listed.** `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` (so `canApplyConfig` and the worker gate), `LIVE_APPLY_FIELDS` and `fieldAppliesLive` in `lib/game-config.ts` are all built from `APPLIER_SPECS`; the worker registry holds the same spec object (`assertConsistent()` throws at boot and in `test/game-config-appliers.test.ts` if the two lists disagree). A schema field that is NOT in the spec is "saved only" and the page says so. The yellow banner "These settings can't be pushed..." disappears for any family with a spec, because `canApplyConfig(family)` becomes true. Kill switch: `NXEON_GAMECFG_APPLIERS=off` (web + worker) turns every registry family back to the old behaviour.
18795-
18796-### The contract
18797-
18798-```ts
18799-// lib/game-config-appliers.ts
18800-type FieldWhen = "live" | "recreate" | "restart";
18801-type FieldApply = { when: FieldWhen; note?: string; secret?: boolean };
18802-type GameConfigApplierSpec = { family: string; fields: Record<schemaKey, FieldApply> };
18803-
18804-// worker/game-config-appliers/types.ts
18805-interface GameConfigApplier { spec: GameConfigApplierSpec; apply(ctx: ApplierContext): Promise<ApplyOutcome>; }
18806-interface ApplierContext {
18807-  family; server: { id; hostname? };
18808-  values: Values;               // validated, fully populated
18809-  changed: string[] | undefined; // keys the customer changed in THIS save; undefined = auto-queued at provision
18810-  touched: string[];            // handled fields in play (handled ∩ changed, or all handled when changed is unknown)
18811-  guest: Guest;                 // exec / readFile (null = absent) / writeFile -- never ssh2 directly
18812-  unit: string | null;          // systemd unit supervising the game container
18813-  waitPort(): Promise<{ ok: boolean } | null>; // uses the family's slow-start window (lib/game-power-start.ts)
18814-  restartRequested: boolean;    // customer chose "Apply & restart"
18815-}
18816-type ApplyOutcome = { ok; applied: string[]; notes: string[]; restarted?: boolean; live?: boolean };
18817-```
18818-
18819-- `when` meanings: `live` = in effect on save with no restart (rcon / live command); `recreate` = applied on save by rebuilding the container (a brief restart is part of it); `restart` = written on save, in effect after the server restarts. The page shows "applies on save", "applies on save, brief restart" and "needs restart" per field, plus the spec `note` under the field. `restartNeeded` in `GameSettings.tsx` (which decides whether "Apply & restart" is offered) is true only for changed `restart` fields.
18820-- **Restart policy.** An applier never decides to restart the game for a `restart` field. `gameConfigApply` (`worker/game-config.ts`) already reconciles run state (restart when the customer asked, "restart needed" note otherwise, stopped servers stay stopped). It now passes `payload.restart` through, and treats `outcome.live === true` as "nothing needs a restart". A `recreate` applier restarts as part of its work and sets `restarted: true`.
18821-- **Result list.** `applied` and `notes` become the post-save notification body (existing path). The runner appends "Saved but not applied to the running game: ..." for every changed field the spec does not handle.
18822-- **Idempotent.** If no changed field belongs to the applier, `apply` is not even called; each strategy no-ops when the guest already matches (`unchanged` / `noop`).
18823-- **Concurrency.** Unchanged: `saveGameConfig` refuses while another job is in flight (`hasInflightJob`), and one GAME_CONFIG job runs per server.
18824-- **Secrets.** Mark credential fields `secret: true`; the runner redacts their values from every `applied`/`notes` string and from thrown errors. The kit never puts values in a command line (env goes through a 0600 env-file, files through SFTP) and error notes are fixed strings (the config-file helper deliberately does not echo parser messages, which can quote file content).
18825-- **Never leave the server stopped.** `recreateWithEnv` keeps the old container as `<name>-old` until the new one is verified; any failure restores it and restarts it if it was running; a half-finished earlier run (only `-old` exists) is healed first. A server the customer had stopped is rebuilt but not started.
18826-
18827-### Strategies (the kit)
18828-
18829-- **config-file** (`patchRemoteFile` + a patcher): read, patch, validate, no-op if identical, `cp -p` backup, write, read back and validate, restore on failure. Returns `restore()` / `commit()` so a later step can still undo it. Patchers: `patchJson` (preserves unknown keys, key order, indent; optional wrapper object such as TShock's `Settings`), `patchIni` (preserves comments, sections, CRLF; appends missing keys in the right section), `updateKeyValue` (server.properties style; moved verbatim from `worker/game-config.ts`).
18830-- **env-recreate** (`recreateWithEnv`): `docker inspect` the old container, build the new `docker create` from its own config (ports, binds, log opts, user, cmd, entrypoint if overridden; only env that differs from the image default is carried), swap, start if it was running, wait for the port, then verify the new container's env/cmd/binds/ports by reading them back. Generalises `worker/zomboid-admin.ts`.
18831-- **rcon/live**: not in the kit yet; use `runRcon` from `worker/game-control.ts` inside your `apply` and return `live: true` when every applied field is live. (First family to need it adds `kit/rcon.ts`.)
18832-- **mixed**: just call several in one `apply` (Terraria does config-file then env-recreate, and restores the file if the recreate fails, so failure always means "nothing changed").
18833-- `verifyReadback(expected, actual)` compares and returns KEY NAMES only.
18834-
18835-### How to add a family (step by step)
18836-
18837-1. Find the truth for the real image: its setup script (`prisma/catalog.ts`, `prisma/seed-wave*.ts`), the image's own docs, and ideally a real container (`docker inspect`, the actual config file). Decide per schema field: env var, launch arg, config file key, rcon, or none. Only mark a field handled if you are confident; everything else stays "saved only".
18838-2. Create `lib/game-applier-specs/<family>.ts`: export `<FAMILY>_SPEC: GameConfigApplierSpec` and any PURE mapping helpers (schema value -> real key/format). Keep it free of node imports (the settings page imports it).
18839-3. Add ONE line to `APPLIER_SPECS` in `lib/game-config-appliers.ts`.
18840-4. Create `worker/game-config-appliers/<family>.ts`: export `<family>Applier: GameConfigApplier = { spec, apply }`. Use the kit; never import `ssh2`, the DB or `worker/game-config.ts`.
18841-5. Add `register(<family>Applier);` in `worker/game-config-appliers/index.ts`.
18842-6. Survive reinstalls: `GAME_REINSTALL` re-runs `buildGameSetupScript` (`worker/game-variant.ts`). If your fields are plain `-e KEY=` env, `applyGameConfigEnv` already bakes them (set `envKey` on the field if the env name differs). Otherwise add a pure `apply<Family>Setup(script, values)` and call it in `buildGameSetupScript` as Terraria does.
18843-7. Update the schema `help` text so it no longer says the field is not applied (`lib/game-config.ts`).
18844-8. Tests with `test/_fake-docker-guest.ts` (extend the fake if you need more docker/systemd behaviour): each mapped field, a no-op re-apply, a failure that rolls back, a secret not leaking, a field the spec does not handle. Copy `test/terraria-applier.test.ts`.
18845-9. `npx tsc --noEmit`, run your tests plus `test/game-config-appliers.test.ts`, fill in the table below, and say honestly what you could not verify against a real server.
18846-

18848-

# TShock 6.2.1 Release Summary

**Terraria Version:** This release adds support for Terraria 1.4.5.8 through an upgrade to OTAPI 3.3.14.

**Docker Image:** Users can access this version via `docker pull ghcr.io/pryaxis/tshock:stable`, which contains the stable TShock release.

**Breaking Changes/Compatibility:** The page does not explicitly detail breaking changes. However, it strongly recommends creating "a complete backup of your existing server and all files and folders, including `tshock.sqlite` and the `tshock` folder" before upgrading.

**Migration/Upgrade Process:** To upgrade, replace all server installation files with those from the release package, overwriting existing files. The documentation assures that "no data will be lost" during this process, though backup verification is emphasized as a precaution.

**Configuration/Database Compatibility:** Specific compatibility details for configurations, databases, or world files are not addressed in this release announcement.

# Dockerfile Content

Here is the complete Dockerfile provided:

```dockerfile
# TARGETPLATFORM and BUILDPLATFORM are automatically filled in by Docker buildx.
# They should not be set in the global scope manually.

FROM --platform=${BUILDPLATFORM} mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:9.0 AS builder

# Install msgfmt for i18n
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y gettext

# Copy build context
WORKDIR /TShock
COPY . ./

# Build and package release based on target architecture
RUN dotnet build -v m
WORKDIR /TShock/TShockLauncher

# Make TARGETPLATFORM available to the container.
ARG TARGETPLATFORM

RUN \ 
  case "${TARGETPLATFORM}" in \
    "linux/amd64") export ARCH="linux-x64" \
    ;; \
    "linux/arm64") export ARCH="linux-arm64" \
    ;; \
    "linux/arm/v7") export ARCH="linux-arm" \
    ;; \
    "windows/amd64") export ARCH="win-x64" \
    ;; \
    *) echo "Error: Unsupported platform ${TARGETPLATFORM}" && exit 1 \
    ;; \
  esac && \
  dotnet publish -o output/ -r "${ARCH}" -v m -f net9.0 -c Release -p:PublishSingleFile=true --self-contained false

# Runtime image
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/runtime:9.0 AS linux_base
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/runtime:9.0-nanoserver-ltsc2022 AS windows_base

FROM ${TARGETOS}_base AS final

WORKDIR /server
COPY --from=builder /TShock/TShockLauncher/output ./

VOLUME ["/tshock", "/worlds", "/plugins"]
EXPOSE 7777 7878

ENTRYPOINT [ \
  "./TShock.Server", \
  "-configpath", "/tshock", \
  "-logpath", "/tshock/logs", \
  "-crashdir", "/tshock/crashes", \
  "-worldselectpath", "/worlds", \
  "-additionalplugins", "/plugins" \
]
```

**Note:** No separate entrypoint or bootstrap script is referenced in this Dockerfile. The ENTRYPOINT directly invokes the compiled application binary.

# TShock -world Parameter Issue Summary

Based on the GitHub issue provided, I can only address what's documented in Issue #1483. The page doesn't contain information about TShock 6, Docker, or any resolution to this problem.

## The Core Problem

The issue describes a bug where TShock ignores the `-world` parameter. When users specify a particular world file via command-line arguments, the server either:

1. **With `-autocreate`**: Generates default worlds (World.wld, World2.wld, etc.) instead of the specified one
2. **Without `-autocreate`**: Crashes with a FileNotFoundException

The reporter notes: *"This suggests the parameter is being listened to by some things and not others,"* indicating inconsistent parameter handling across the codebase.

## What's Missing

The page doesn't include:
- Any documented resolution or fix
- TShock 6 or Docker-specific guidance
- Follow-up comments or workarounds
- Closure status or related PRs

To find current solutions, you'd need to check TShock's documentation, later issues, or pull requests addressing this bug.

# Command-Line Argument Parsing in TShock

## Parsing Mechanism

The code uses a `CommandLineParser` with flag-based parsing. Key arguments are processed in `HandleCommandLine()` and `HandleCommandLinePostConfigLoad()` methods.

## Arguments and Their Handling

**Pre-Config Arguments** (in `HandleCommandLine`):
- `-configpath`: Sets `SavePath` directory for TShock data
- `-worldselectpath`: Sets `Main.WorldPath` for world selection
- `-logpath`: Sets `LogPath` for log files
- `-logformat`: Customizes log filename format
- `-autocreate`: Calls `Main.instance.autoCreate(size)` with the provided size parameter
- `-worldname`: Calls `Main.instance.SetWorldName(world)`
- `-port`: Sets `Netplay.ListenPort`
- `-ip`: Validates and sets `Netplay.ServerIP`
- `-config`: Loads a dedicated config file via `Main.instance.LoadDedConfig()`

**Post-Config Arguments** (in `HandleCommandLinePostConfigLoad`):
- `-port`: Overrides config setting; sets `OverridePort = true`
- `-maxplayers`/`-players`: Sets `Config.Settings.MaxSlots`
- `--rest-token`/`-rest-token`: Populates `RESTStartupTokens`
- `--rest-enabled`/`-rest-enabled`: Toggles `Config.Settings.RestApiEnabled`
- `--rest-port`/`-rest-port`: Sets `Config.Settings.RestApiPort`

## Config File Interactions

**ServerPassword**: CLI-defined password takes precedence. The code stores CLI password in `_cliPassword` and prevents config reloads from overriding it: `"This prevents a config reload from removing/updating a CLI-defined password"`

**MaxSlots**: Config specifies max players; CLI argument via `-maxplayers` overrides this value post-config-load.

This version adds support for Terraria 1.4.5.8. Thank you so much for all of the hard work that went into this release!

## Notable changes in this release

- Upgraded to OTAPI 3.3.14 for Terraria 1.4.5.8. (@ZakFahey, @bulkinglb, @sors89, @timschumi, @SignatureBeef, @QuiCM, @lost-werewolf)

## Upgrading

**Before installing, make a complete backup of your existing server and all files and folders, including `tshock.sqlite` and the `tshock` folder. We are not responsible for failed installations. Please make sure you backup your data. Severe data loss or gain may occur.**

To upgrade TShock, replace all of the files in the location of your server installation with all of the files from the release zip we provide. Overwrite all files. No data will be lost.

## Docker

Users of Docker may consider using ` docker pull ghcr.io/pryaxis/tshock:stable` to get this release. `stable` contains the stable version of TShock.

content.thinking:
I need to be careful here: the GAME_UPDATE job currently runs every 6h for autoUpdate servers and on manual "Update now" requests. If I hook terraria's image update into that automatic sweep, it would silently roll out updates to all customers' servers at once, which isn't what the owner wants. Instead, I should gate the terraria update so it only triggers on a manual job or an explicit payload flag, preserving one-by-one rollout control.

I'm settling on gating the terraria update so it only fires when payload.terrariaImageUpdate is explicitly true, or when an environment flag like NXEON_TERRARIA_AUTO_UPDATE is turned on for sweep-wide rollout, defaulting to off so nothing changes automatically. For the owner's manual rollout, I'll provide a small script to enqueue a one-off GAME_UPDATE job for a specific server with that flag set, plus a separate sweep/admin check that just reports version drift between running and pinned Terraria versions without actually updating anything.

For the drift check I'm designing a function that SSHes into each Terraria server, reads the running image and version, and returns a report — paired with an admin script to run it on demand. I'm keeping this report-only, exported as a function plus a script rather than wiring it into a live scheduler, to avoid unintended production side effects.

Now I'm writing the core terraria-image library: pinning the image repo, TShock version, vanilla version, and digest into a single reference string, adding a legacy-image detector for the old ryshe/terraria path, and defining a mapping function that converts old bind mounts to the new container's expected paths.

I'm also working out how old container commands and environment variables need to transform for the new image — dropping duplicate plugin flags since the new entrypoint already handles that path, converting the old world filename env into a `-world` command argument, and making sure the new container only inherits user-set environment variables rather than carrying over the old image's bootstrap-specific env and entrypoint.

Rather than reusing the existing env-recreate logic as-is, I'm thinking about extending it with new optional parameters for a different target image, custom bind computation, entrypoint resetting, and post-start verification — and when a new image is involved, I'll need to inspect that image directly to compute its default environment and entrypoint for comparison, rather than assuming it matches the current container's image.

For carrying over environment variables, I'll keep comparing against the old image's defaults to detect user-set overrides, explicitly nulling out WORLD_FILENAME, and add an image-mismatch check to the noop detection so a differing target image always forces a recreate. For safety, I'm planning a pre-upgrade backup of /opt/terraria via a guest-side copy (checking free space first since worlds can be sizable), preserving the plugins directory, and using that backup to roll back world/database files if the new container ends up migrating or corrupting them on boot.

For the rollback sequence, I need to make sure data restoration happens before the old container restarts -- so I'll add an onRollback hook that runs right after the failed container is stopped/renamed but before the old one comes back up, moving the failed state aside and restoring from backup. The old image itself can just stay untouched for simplicity. For verifying a successful update, I'll check the container logs for TShock's startup banner and a "world loaded" confirmation, though I'm not fully certain of the exact log line format TShock prints on boot.

I'll build tolerant regex patterns that match version strings for both TShock and vanilla Terraria server, plus a "world loaded" check combining "Server started" with the absence of failure markers like aborted startup, unhandled exceptions, or file-not-found errors -- while noting these patterns are based on the brief's description rather than a confirmed real log sample.

If the log format doesn't match expectations and parsing fails, the conservative default is to roll back rather than proceed, which is the safe failure mode. For stopped containers I'll skip log verification entirely and rely only on inspect data for image, binds, and command. I need to add a verification hook that runs after the container is recreated and its state read back, since the old container is already gone by that point -- if verification fails, this triggers a rollback that restores data through an onRollback callback; I also need to account for slow-starting containers by polling logs for up to about a minute rather than checking just once.

Before touching anything I want to pull the image first with a generous timeout, so a failed pull means nothing has changed yet. I'm also considering a disk space check comparing available space against double the current data size before proceeding, though I want to keep this simple. For testing, the shared fake guest doesn't support all these new commands (pull, logs, backup copies, disk usage checks, sleep), and since that fake is used by other tests I don't want to modify it heavily -- instead I'm leaning toward wrapping it so I can intercept my new commands while delegating everything else through to the original implementation.

I'm working out how the fake's file system and container state should behave for directory copies and image inspection, noting that the fake hard-codes entrypoint values which shouldn't matter for my verification logic since I'm not checking entrypoint. For the logs command, I want the wrapper to return different text depending on which image the current container is actually running, pulling that from the fake's container state. Now I'm also tracing through how the fake parses `docker create` arguments to find the image reference and trailing command args, making sure flags with values don't get mistaken for the image position.

For rollback, since the command splitter doesn't recognize `mv` as a special token, I'll break the restore sequence into separate exec calls for `mv` and `cp -a` so the wrapper can intercept each one individually, keeping the old world directory renamed aside rather than deleted so data is never lost.

For verifying backup integrity, I'm considering comparing file counts between source and backup directories using `find` and `wc -l`, though that requires the wrapper to recognize a special marker — a simpler alternative would be using `diff -rq` to check directory equality directly.

But I realize the real issue is timing: sqlite world files could be mid-write during an autosave when backup runs, so the backup should ideally happen after the server process has stopped, not while it's live. I'm thinking I need an `afterStop` hook that runs after the old container is stopped and renamed but before the new one starts, so backups are taken on a quiescent filesystem, with any failure there triggering the existing rollback path.

Verification can use a recursive diff check between source and backup, with a timestamped backup path under /opt that's left for manual cleanup. I'm also flagging a plugin compatibility risk: older customer plugins built against prior OTAPI/TShock versions might fail to load on a newer server version, so the verify step needs to catch that kind of startup abort too.

I need to check whether any of the three servers actually has plugins installed, since that determines if this risk even applies. I'm also comparing the config and log paths between the ryshe and official images—both seem to map to the same host locations (/opt/terraria/config.json, /opt/terraria/logs), which is reassuring since it means the config applier doesn't need changes. Similarly, the tshock.sqlite database should live at the same relative path under SavePath in both setups, and I'm now tracing how the world file argument gets passed to the server binary to confirm the world path translates correctly between the two images.

For new servers, I'm worried about whether `-world` with autocreate reliably produces a deterministically named world file, since the switching logic depends on exact filenames—but I can't verify this without actually running the image, and I'm wary of running a throwaway container on what might be a production host. I should just check whether docker is even installed on this box before going further.

#!/bin/bash

echo "\nBootstrap:\nworld_file_name=$WORLD_FILENAME\nconfigpath=$CONFIGPATH\nlogpath=$LOGPATH\n"

# Copy plugins if the folder is empty (like on first run)
if [ -z "$(ls -A /tshock/ServerPlugins)" ]; then
  echo "Copying plugins..."
  cp /plugins/* /tshock/ServerPlugins
fi

if [ $(jq -r '.Settings.StorageType' $CONFIGPATH/config.json) = "mysql" ]; then
  DATABASE_SERVER=$(jq -r '.Settings.MySqlHost' $CONFIGPATH/config.json | cut -f1 -d':')
  DATABASE_PORT=$(jq -r '.Settings.MySqlHost' $CONFIGPATH/config.json | cut -f2 -d':')
  DATABASE_USER_NAME=$(jq -r '.Settings.MySqlUsername' $CONFIGPATH/config.json)
  DATABASE_USER_PASSWORD=$(jq -r '.Settings.MySqlPassword' $CONFIGPATH/config.json)
  echo "Waiting for the database server."
  while ! mysql -h$DATABASE_SERVER -P$DATABASE_PORT -u$DATABASE_USER_NAME -p$DATABASE_USER_PASSWORD -e ";"; do
    sleep 0.1
  done
fi

WORLD_PATH="/root/.local/share/Terraria/Worlds/$WORLD_FILENAME"

autocreate_flag=false
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ "$arg" = "-autocreate" ]; then
    autocreate_flag=true
    break
  fi
done

if [ -z "$WORLD_FILENAME" ]; then
  echo "No world file specified in environment WORLD_FILENAME."
  if [ -z "$@" ]; then
    echo "Running server setup..."
  else
    echo "Running server with command flags: $@"
  fi
  ./TShock.Server -configpath "$CONFIGPATH" -logpath "$LOGPATH" "$@"
else
  echo "Environment WORLD_FILENAME specified"
  if [ -f "$WORLD_PATH" ] || [ "$autocreate_flag" = true ]; then
    echo "Loading to world $WORLD_FILENAME..."
    ./TShock.Server -configpath "$CONFIGPATH" -logpath "$LOGPATH" -world "$WORLD_PATH" "$@"
  else
    echo "Unable to locate $WORLD_PATH and -autocreate flag is not set."
    echo "Please make sure your world file is volumed into docker: -v <path_to_world_file>:/root/.local/share/Terraria/Worlds"
    echo "Alternatively, use the -autocreate flag to create a new world."
    exit 1
  fi
fi

 * INTERACTIVE world-selection menu ("n  New World / d <number>  Delete
 * World") and waits forever on a stdin that never comes, so the game never
 * binds 7777. With WORLD_FILENAME set but no world file and no -autocreate

content.thinking:
Now I'm designing the mirror sweep function for worker/terraria-mirror.ts, which checks if mirroring is disabled first, then ensures the root directory exists before proceeding with the sweep logic.

It fetches TShock releases from GitHub and ghcr tags, falling back to the existing index if either request fails. Then it builds a catalogue merging new data with preserved mirror facts, determines which versions are in-use by querying active servers' tshock versions, and plans downloads for kept-but-unmirrored versions using skopeo to copy images locally, followed by verification of the downloaded tarball's checksum, size, and image ID from its manifest.

For drift detection, there's a separate sweep that SSHes into running Terraria servers to inspect version drift and compares it against the recommended version from the catalogue or a pinned override, scheduling this as a recurring job.

I'm weighing whether this should be gated behind an environment flag or on by default — read-only inspection every 6 hours seems benign, but I want to make sure any admin notification about drift doesn't trigger external sends like email or Discord, since the policy restricts those channels.

I'll have the sweep write a simple `drift.json` report plus console log instead of adding a database schema, keeping a small script for the admin to check rather than building a full admin page. For the mirror sweep, I'll default it off behind a `TERRARIA_MIRROR_SWEEP` flag so the owner has to opt in, since downloading files to disk repeatedly is a prod-affecting decision I shouldn't make default-on.

I'm settling on: mirror sweep default off since it writes to disk and uses network, while the drift sweep stays default on since it's read-only, and the owner can trigger a mirror manually right away.

I need a guest adapter that wraps SSH exec calls for reading and writing files on the remote server using simple shell commands like `cat` and `test -f`, rather than relying on sftp like the existing config path does. Now I'm looking at where to wire this into the game-update flow, right after the check that the server is running.

For the terraria branch in game-update, I'm routing jobs flagged for terraria updates (either explicitly in the payload or via an env toggle) to a dedicated job handler, keeping the main update file lean. That handler needs to resolve the target version from the payload, catalogue, or pinned default, share the resolveTarget logic by moving it into its own module, then use the SSH connection with the guest adapter to actually perform the image update and wait for the port to come back up.

For determining the systemd unit name, I'm probing with `systemctl cat` to confirm "terraria.service" exists before using it elsewhere for status checks like `is-active`.

For handling the outcome, I'm recording the update result, logging to the audit trail, notifying the customer in-app for success/failure cases (skipping notification when already current), and alerting admins specifically when a failed update also failed to roll back successfully. On failure I also mark the job as no-retry before rethrowing.

I also need to update the stored game config version only on success, keep this gated to RUNNING servers, and handle customer-stopped states as the kit already does. Time to actually write out worker/terraria-job.ts, terraria-guest.ts, and terraria-target.ts, then sweep through the other files to wire everything together.

I found the actual bug: the path-prefix check for the backup directory doesn't match because it requires an exact "dirname + /" prefix, and "/opt/terraria-backup..." doesn't fall under "/opt/terraria/" by that rule. So the manifest meant for the backup folder ends up written into the main terraria directory instead.

Tracing further, I realize in the startFailsForNew scenario the rollback flag gets set true before the new start attempt, so the restore logic runs and copies the backup (including the leftover manifest file) back over the host directory — which is why the manifest shows up where it shouldn't.

To fix this, I should write the manifest file next to the backup folder as `${backup}.txt` rather than inside it, and adjust my test expectations since restoring here is actually harmless (just a redundant identical copy) — I'll update the assertions to confirm data integrity and the existence of the failed directory rather than expecting no restore at all.

cd /tank/nxeon-wt-terraria-update && cat >> docs/DOCUMENTATION.md <<'EOF'

### Terraria image update, version catalogue and local mirror (2026-10-02, branch `fix/terraria-tshock-update`)

**Why.** Terraria 1.4.5.8 shipped; every Nxeon Terraria server ran `ryshe/terraria:latest` (TShock 6.1.0.0 / Terraria 1.4.5.6, sha256:b1c89f7f...), so players on the current client could not join. That image's TShock line is unmaintained (Docker Hub's newest TShock tag is `tshock-1.4.5.6-6.1.0`, 2026-03-11; only its vanilla tags move). TShock publishes an official image, `ghcr.io/pryaxis/tshock:<release>` (6.2.1 = Terraria 1.4.5.8, 2026-09-27). New servers and every updated server now run it, pinned to an explicit tag (never `latest`). **Not yet confirmed on a real server: all of this was built against fakes and read off the registry/repo, no real update was run.**

**One place for the version.** `lib/terraria-image.ts`: `TERRARIA_PINNED_VERSION` (+ a verified row in `TERRARIA_KNOWN_VERSIONS` with the Terraria version, image id, registry index digest). Bump it for new servers and the drift reference. Also `lib/terraria-plugins.ts` `TERRARIA_SETUP_SCRIPT` derives its tag from it.

**Container contract (read with skopeo + ryshe's `bootstrap.sh` extracted from its layer).**

| | `ryshe/terraria` (legacy) | `ghcr.io/pryaxis/tshock` |
|---|---|---|
| entrypoint | `/bin/sh bootstrap.sh` | `./TShock.Server -configpath /tshock -logpath /tshock/logs -crashdir /tshock/crashes -worldselectpath /worlds -additionalplugins /plugins` |
| world file | env `WORLD_FILENAME` -> `-world <Worlds>/<file>` | we pass `-world /worlds/<file>` (+ `-autocreate N -worldname X` as before) |
| worlds / config dirs | `/root/.local/share/Terraria/Worlds` (it is also CONFIGPATH: config.json and tshock.sqlite sit beside the .wld files) | `/worlds`, `/tshock` |
| cwd (for plugins opening `tshock/<f>`) | `/tshock` (so `/tshock/tshock` alias) | `/server` (so `/server/tshock` alias) |
| plugins | `/tshock/CustomPlugins` + `-additionalplugins` in Cmd | `/plugins` (flag already in the entrypoint) |
| user / ports | root / 7777 (7878 exposed) | root / 7777 (7878 exposed), volumes `/tshock /worlds /plugins` |

On our guests every host path is the same folder, `/opt/terraria`, so the on-disk layout does not change (`config.json` stays `/opt/terraria/config.json`; the existing config applier is untouched). Only mount points differ: `/opt/terraria` is mounted at `/worlds`, `/tshock` and `/server/tshock`, `/opt/terraria-plugins` at `/plugins`. 6.0.0, 6.1.0, 6.2.0 and 6.2.1 carry the identical contract. Compatibility: TShock's 6.2.1 notes say "replace the files, no data will be lost" and to back up `tshock.sqlite` and the `tshock` folder; TShock fills missing config keys and migrates its db itself. Terraria worlds are forward compatible in 1.4.x but NOT backward (1.4.5.8 may save a world 1.4.5.6 cannot read), which is why the update backs up first, restores on rollback, and refuses to move a server to a lower Terraria version.

**The update (`worker/terraria-update.ts`, `terrariaImageUpdate`).** 1) read the container, refuse a downgrade or an anonymous-volume world; 2) space check (needs 2x the data + 0.5 GB), then image onto the guest: local mirror tarball (sha256-checked, `docker load`) first, registry fallback (`docker pull repo@indexDigest` then tag), image id verified against the table before anything is stopped; 3) `recreateWithEnv` (extended with `image`, `binds`, `afterStop`, `verify`, `onRollback` hooks; legacy `WORLD_FILENAME` env dropped, cmd rewritten by `terrariaOfficialCmd`): stop, keep the old container as `terraria-old`, **back up `/opt/terraria` to `/opt/terraria-backup-pre-tshock-<ver>-<UTC stamp>` while the game is stopped (cp -a + diff -rq verified; a restore note beside it as `<backup>.txt`)**, create the new container with the same ports and mapped volumes, start it ONLY if it was running, wait for the port (slow-start window), read it back, then poll `docker logs` for `TShock <ver>` + `Terraria Server v<ver>` + `Server started` with no abort marker and the world file present; 4) any failure: new container removed, old one renamed back, and if the new one had been started the data folder is moved to `/opt/terraria-failed-<stamp>` and the backup copied back, then the old container is restarted (if it was running). A server the customer stopped stays stopped (recreated, not started; the drift report proves its version after the next start). The log patterns are matched loosely (`TShock v?6.2.1(.0)`, `Terraria Server v1.4.5.8`) because the exact 6.2.1 banner was not available without running it: if it differs, the update FAILS SAFE (rollback), it never passes on a guess.

**How it is triggered.** `GAME_UPDATE` with payload `{ terrariaUpdate: true, version? }` (`worker/game-update.ts` -> `worker/terraria-job.ts`); `scripts/terraria-enqueue-update.ts <host|id> [--version X] [--apply]` creates exactly one such job (dry run by default). The 6-hourly sweep only does it when `NXEON_TERRARIA_AUTO_UPDATE=on` (default off) and the customer opted in. A customer can also pick a version in Settings (`tshock-version`, applier `when: recreate`); a Settings save that does not change that field never touches the image, and the auto-queued post-provision apply never updates it. On success the job also stores the version in `Server.gameConfig["tshock-version"]` so the picker shows what runs.

**Catalogue + local mirror.** `lib/terraria-versions.ts` builds the list from GitHub releases of Pryaxis/TShock (asset name `TShock-<v>-for-Terraria-<t>-linux-x64-Release.zip` = the Terraria version) intersected with the ghcr tag list; pre-releases and anything below 6.0.0 are never offered; the newest stable with an image is `recommended`. `worker/terraria-mirror.ts` (`terrariaMirrorSweep`, 6-hourly, inert unless `TERRARIA_MIRROR_SWEEP=on`; or run `scripts/terraria-mirror-sync.ts` once) refreshes it into `/tank/nxlabs-mirror/terraria/index.json` and downloads the kept versions (recommended + newest 3 + every version a server uses) with `skopeo copy --override-arch amd64 ... docker-archive:` to `/tank/nxlabs-mirror/terraria/<ver>/tshock-<ver>.tar` (sha256 + size recorded, image id read back from the tarball and compared with the verified table; mismatches are quarantined). It never deletes a file (`mayEvict` is the one rule for any future eviction: never in-use, never recommended), never creates the dataset root, and reports releases missing from `TERRARIA_KNOWN_VERSIONS` (add the row it prints: a version without a verified image id is not orderable). Guests download through `/api/tshock-image/<hmac-token>/<ver>/tshock-<ver>.tar` (`lib/terraria-mirror-serve.ts`, same model as `/api/mcjars`: per-file token, range, ETag, rate limit, stream cap, 404 for anything unlisted), reachable from game guests via nxeon.cloud. `/api/terraria-versions` feeds the Settings picker (version, Terraria version, release date, notes, recommended); without a catalogue it falls back to the built-in verified list. Kill switch `TERRARIA_MIRROR_DISABLED=1`.

**Design decision, mirror format.** Option (a) mirrored `docker save`-style tarball of the official image (chosen) vs (b) an Nxeon launcher on a .NET runtime base with the TShock zip mounted read-only. (b) still needs the `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/runtime` base from a registry (or its own saved tarball), adds a launcher we must maintain and patch, and changes the container contract for plugins/worlds on all 3 servers; its only gain (swap a mounted zip) is already a recreate in (a). (a) keeps TShock's own supported image and entrypoint, makes a version change "load tarball + recreate" (what the update path already does), and `skopeo` (already on the primary) produces the archive without a docker daemon. Fallback is always a registry pull by digest, so the mirror can only help.

TERRARIA TSHOCK UPDATE — REPORT

Branch fix/terraria-tshock-update, worktree /tank/nxeon-wt-terraria-update (from feature/game-config-apply-core; real node_modules copy). One commit 9d7dbf534f (not pushed). Notes: /root/agent-notes/terraria-update.md. Docs: docs/DOCUMENTATION.md, section "Terraria image update, version catalogue and local mirror". Merge order: feature/game-config-apply-core first (this branch builds on it). No schema change. Nothing was deployed, no node, VM or prod DB was touched, and no real update was run. The only outside contact was read-only registry/GitHub reads (skopeo inspect, GitHub API, a copy of ryshe's image layer into scratch, since deleted).

1. RESEARCH FINDINGS
- ryshe/terraria is not maintained for TShock. Its newest TShock tag is tshock-1.4.5.6-6.1.0 (2026-03-11); only its vanilla tags moved (vanilla-1.4.5.8, 2026-08-24).
- Chosen image: the official ghcr.io/pryaxis/tshock:6.2.1 (published 2026-09-27, Terraria 1.4.5.8).
  - Registry values read via skopeo: index digest sha256:70e59a8e6b4c79b5fad469d320962c1fc98625ed3a955510a2f2641dbff2f7e7, amd64 image id sha256:9b5081fd957d1a6565a80b4d16f850e41c75e76070c8375d9e2e902f111b7a00, about 109 MB compressed.
  - It runs as root with WorkingDir /server. Volumes are /tshock, /worlds and /plugins; ports 7777 and 7878 are exposed.
  - Entrypoint: ./TShock.Server -configpath /tshock -logpath /tshock/logs -crashdir /tshock/crashes -worldselectpath /worlds -additionalplugins /plugins. It has no bootstrap script. Tags 6.0.0, 6.1.0, 6.2.0 and 6.2.1 carry the same contract.
- Old contract, read from ryshe's extracted bootstrap.sh: the WORLD_FILENAME env becomes `-world <Worlds>/<file>`. CONFIGPATH is the Worlds folder, so config.json and tshock.sqlite sit next to the .wld files. The working directory is /tshock, which explains the /tshock/tshock alias.
- New contract: we pass `-world /worlds/<file>` ourselves, plus the same -autocreate/-worldname as before.
- On our guests every host path is the same folder, /opt/terraria. The on-disk layout is unchanged and config.json stays /opt/terraria/config.json, so the existing config applier still works.
- Mount mapping: /opt/terraria goes to /worlds, /tshock and /server/tshock. The /server/tshock alias replaces the old /tshock/tshock one for plugins that open "tshock/<file>". /opt/terraria-plugins goes to /plugins, and the -additionalplugins arg is dropped because the entrypoint already has it.
- Compatibility: TShock's release notes say "replace the files, no data will be lost" and tell people to back up tshock.sqlite and the tshock folder. TShock fills missing config keys and migrates its own db. Terraria worlds are forward compatible in 1.4.x but not backward, so the update backs up first, restores on rollback, and refuses a move to a lower Terraria version.

2. WHAT WAS BUILT
- lib/terraria-image.ts (new): the single place for the pinned version, TERRARIA_PINNED_VERSION = "6.2.1" (a one-line bump), plus a verified TERRARIA_KNOWN_VERSIONS table with image id and index digest. It also holds the contract mappers (cmd, binds), the log parsers and the drift judge.
- worker/terraria-update.ts (new), `terrariaImageUpdate`:
  - Preflight: refuses a downgrade or a world folder that is not a host bind, then checks free space (2x data + 0.5 GB).
  - Image: from the mirror tarball (sha256-checked, docker load) first, else `docker pull repo@digest` plus tag. The image id is verified before anything is stopped.
  - Recreate: reuses recreateWithEnv, extended with `image`, `binds`, `afterStop`, `verify` and `onRollback` hooks. The backup is cp -a plus diff -rq to /opt/terraria-backup-pre-tshock-<ver>-<stamp>, taken while the game is stopped.
  - Start and verify: the new container is started only if the server was running. Then it waits for the port and polls `docker logs` for "TShock <ver>", "Terraria Server v<ver>" and "Server started" with no abort marker, and checks the world file exists.
  - Rollback: on any failure the new container is removed and the old one renamed back. If the new one had started, the data folder is moved aside and the backup copied back. The old container is restarted if it was running.
  - A server the customer stopped is recreated but stays stopped, and its logs are not polled.
- Wiring: GAME_UPDATE with payload {terrariaUpdate:true, version?} goes through worker/game-update.ts to worker/terraria-job.ts.
  - Job result: the customer is notified, the audit log is written, and gameConfig["tshock-version"] is stored on success. noRetry applies on failure.
  - The automatic sweep only does this if NXEON_TERRARIA_AUTO_UPDATE=on (default off).
